headline: Trump says his giant arch will hold snipers and drones
summary: President Trump said Sunday that the 250-foot arch he wants between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery will double as a military complex: drones and snipers on the roof and plaza, ammunition in storage. He says the military asked. The Pentagon had nothing to add. A lawsuit says Congress must approve it.

cover_question.q: Why would an arch have soldiers in it?

cover_answer: He says the military asked. The Pentagon had nothing to add.
table_question: Should a monument do a second job, or just stand there?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president wants to build a huge stone arch near Washington, half as tall as the Washington Monument. On Sunday he said soldiers would use it too, to keep watch from the top. It isn't built yet, and lots of grown-ups still have to say yes. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A tall thing and a job for it. A five-year-old can picture both, and “not built yet” is the reassurance.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them a height they can picture, half the Washington Monument, and one plain job for the building. The lawsuit and the Pentagon's silence stay out. Expect “can we go up it?” Not yet: it is a plan, and lots of people still have to agree.

8-12.script: Trump wants to build a 250-foot arch in Washington, and on Sunday he said it will also hold drones and snipers. He says the military asked; the Pentagon had nothing to add. It's a permission slip with several signatures: a commission still has to vote, and a lawsuit says Congress must too.
8-12.why: A chain with a gap in it, and a permission slip they have carried.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults follow the rules, so the script gives them the chain: a plan, a new claim about it, and the signatures it still needs. The permission slip is the mechanism. Expect “can he just do it?” Not on his own. A commission still has to vote, and a lawsuit says Congress must too.

13-17.script: What do you make of it when the president says the military asked for something and the Pentagon says it has nothing to add? Trump says his arch will hold drones and snipers because the military asked. Second: if a project is called national security, should it need the same approvals?
13-17.why: Two claims that don't quite meet. Let them decide what the gap means.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is not in front of them, and this story is that: a claim from the president, silence from the Pentagon, and a label now on two buildings. The script hands them the gap, not a verdict. Expect “so is he lying?” Say what is known, then ask what would count as evidence.

5-7.q: Why would an arch have soldiers in it?
5-7.a: He says the army asked for a place to keep watch from. It isn't built yet, and lots of people still have to say yes.

8-12.q: Can the president just build whatever he wants?
8-12.a: No. A commission still has to vote, and a lawsuit says Congress must too.
Half the Washington Monument. Two and a half Lincoln Memorials.

13-17.q: Did the military really ask for it?
13-17.a: He says so. The Pentagon said it had no information beyond his statement.

13-17.q: Why does it matter what he calls it?
13-17.a: He called the ballroom one too. BBC says the approvals are unclear.
